passages.title: The oath and the deniers' astonishment
passages.tafsir:
Sūrah Qāf opens with a single letter and a solemn oath by the Qur'an itself, and then immediately shows us the reaction of those who heard it: not argument, but astonishment. These five ayat form one tight movement — Allah swears by His own Book, reports the deniers' double amazement (that a human being should warn them, and that the dead should live again), answers their objection with a statement about His own knowledge, and finally exposes the real reason underneath their objection. The oath at the start and the diagnosis at the end are two ends of the same argument.

## The sūrah the Prophet ﷺ recited every Friday

Before the words themselves, it helps to know how central this sūrah was to the Prophet's ﷺ public life.

Imam Ahmad recorded that 'Umar bin Al-Khattab asked Abu Waqid Al-Laythi what the Prophet ﷺ used to recite in the 'Id prayer. He answered: Sūrah Qāf and Sūrat Iqtarabat (that is, Sūrah Al-Qamar, chapter 54). Ibn Kathir notes that Muslim and the Four Collectors of the Sunan also collected this.

Imam Ahmad also recorded from Umm Hisham bint Harithah — collected by Muslim — a detail so domestic it is easy to miss: "For around two years, or a year and a part of another year, our oven and the oven of the Prophet ﷺ was one and the same. I memorized Sūrah *Qāf. Wal-Qur'ānil-Majīd* from the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who used to recite it every Friday while standing on the Minbar delivering the Friday sermon to the people." Abu Dawud recorded something similar from the daughter of Al-Harith bin An-Nu'man: "I only memorized Sūrah Qāf from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who used to recite it in every Friday Khutbah. Our oven and the oven of the Messenger ﷺ was one and the same" — this too was collected by Muslim and An-Nasa'i.

Sit with that picture. A woman whose household shared an oven with the Prophet's ﷺ household learned this sūrah by heart from his tongue — from hearing him recite it, week after week, from the pulpit. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, from Qurtubi, that Jabir reported the Prophet ﷺ often recited Sūrah Qāf in the Morning Prayer, and that although the sūrah is rather long, the prayer felt light — it was a special trait of his recitation that praying behind him caused no stress even when he recited the long sūrahs.

Why this sūrah, in the largest gatherings of the community — the 'Ids and the Friday sermons? Ibn Kathir answers: because it contains news of the beginning of creation, the Resurrection, the Return, the Standing before Allah, the Reckoning, Paradise, the Fire, Allah's reward and punishment, and lessons of both encouragement and discouragement. It is, in other words, the whole shape of a human being's destiny in a single recitation — exactly what a crowd gathered for celebration or for the weekly sermon most needs to hear.

Ibn Kathir also notes that this sūrah is the first sūrah of the *Mufassal* section of the Qur'an "according to the correct view." (*Mufassal* is the name of one of the sections the Companions used when they divided the Qur'an into parts, as the report below shows.) He records that some said the Mufassal begins with Sūrah Al-Hujurat (49), and that some common people say it begins with Sūrah An-Naba' (78) — an opinion he rejects, because none of the respected scholars ever supported it. His evidence is the report of Aws bin Hudhayfah, who said: "I asked the Companions of Allah's Messenger ﷺ how they divided the Qur'an. They said: 'Three, five, seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, and the Mufassal section as one.'" This was recorded by Ibn Majah and Imam Ahmad. Count those groups out from Al-Baqarah and you reach forty-eight sūrahs, ending at Al-Hujurat (49) — so the Mufassal begins with Qāf.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds why Qāf follows Al-Hujurat so naturally: this sūrah is mostly about the Day of Judgment, Resurrection, the Reckoning, Paradise, the Fire, and Allah's reward and punishment — and the concluding part of Al-Hujurat dealt with these same subjects.

## Ayah 1: a letter, and an oath

**Qāf.** Ibn Kathir treats it as one of the letters of the alphabet mentioned at the beginning of some sūrahs, exactly like *Ṣād* (38:1), *Nūn* (68:1), *Alif Lām Mīm* (2:1), *Ḥā Mīm* (40:1) and *Ṭā Sīn Mīm* (28:1) — this is what Mujahid and several others said. He does not expand on it here, noting that he already discussed these letters at the beginning of his explanation of Sūrah Al-Baqarah and so need not repeat it. There is something instructive in that: a believer is not required to have a theory about these letters in order to benefit from the sūrah they introduce.

**"By the glorious Qur'an."** Ibn Kathir glosses the oath as being by "the Honorable and Great Qur'an." And he immediately reaches for another ayah to fill out what that greatness means: a Book of which Allah says that "falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it: (it is) sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise" (41:42). So the thing being sworn by is not merely impressive; it is untouchable by falsehood from any direction.

Notice what is happening. Allah is about to report people who found the message strange. Before a word of their objection is quoted, He swears by the very Book they are dismissing. The oath places the Qur'an's own majesty on the scales opposite their astonishment — and it is no contest.

## The oath whose subject is carried in the meaning

Here is a point Ibn Kathir draws out that unlocks the passage. The subject of the oath in this ayah, he explains, is specified afterwards even though it does not appear by word — and what it emphasizes is prophethood and resurrection, affirming that they are true. He notes that there are similar oaths in the Qur'an whose subject is included in the meaning but not in the wording, and gives a parallel case: "Ṣād. By the Qur'an full of reminding. Nay, those who disbelieve are in false pride and opposition" (38:1–2).

The effect is powerful. We move straight from "By the glorious Qur'an" to "Nay, they wonder…" The conclusion is never spelled out in words, and the reader supplies it from the meaning. What is being sworn to is so evident from the Book being sworn by that it does not need saying; what needs saying is how astonishing it is that anyone finds it strange.

## Ayat 2–3: two astonishments

Ayah 2 reports the first shock: "Nay, they wonder that there has come to them a warner from among themselves. So the disbelievers say: 'This is a strange thing!'" Ibn Kathir's comment is precise: **they wondered at the wisdom behind sending a Messenger who is a human being.** The offence was not that Allah should send guidance, but that He should send it through a warner from among themselves — one of their own.

Allah answers that elsewhere, in words Ibn Kathir cites here: "Is it a wonder for mankind that We have sent Our revelation to a man from among themselves (saying): 'Warn mankind'" (10:2) — meaning, as he puts it, this is not strange at all, for Allah chooses Messengers from angels and humans.

Ayah 3 gives the second shock, and now they speak for themselves: "When we are dead and have become dust — that is a far return." Ibn Kathir unpacks the reasoning behind the sentence: *after we die, disintegrate, with our organs torn apart and we become dust, how can we be brought back to our original shape and bodies?* And "that is a far return" carries their verdict: it is not likely that it will ever occur. They thought Resurrection was far from happening and would never occur.

Read the two ayat together and a pattern shows. In ayah 2 they call the messenger strange; in ayah 3 they call the message impossible. Both objections are really the same instinct dressed differently: measuring what Allah can do by what they are used to seeing.

## Ayah 4: "We know"

The reply, when it comes, is startling in what it does *not* do. Allah does not begin by describing His power to rebuild bodies. He begins with His knowledge: "We know that which the earth takes of them, and with Us is a Book preserved."

Ibn Kathir explains: *We know what the earth consumes of their dead bodies* — where and how the bodies disintegrated, what they turned into and how they have become. All of this is never absent from Allah's knowledge. Al-'Awfi narrated that 'Abdullah bin 'Abbas commented on this phrase: "It refers to what the earth consumes of their flesh, skin, bones and hair." Ibn Kathir records a similar view from Mujahid, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak and several others; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise reports this interpretation of "diminishing by the earth" from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and the majority of the interpreters, citing Al-Bahr-ul-Muhit.

And then: **"and with Us is a Book preserved."** Ibn Kathir reads it as the record that keeps all records: Allah's knowledge is encompassing, and the Book of decrees has everything precisely recorded in it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies this with the Preserved Tablet, adding that Allah had perfect and full knowledge of every person's destiny even before creating him — what transformation would come about in every moment of his life, and what phases he would go through after his death — all of it precisely recorded there.

Why answer a question about *power* with a statement about *knowledge*? Because the objection in ayah 3 assumed that scattered dust is *lost*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān meets that assumption head on: man's knowledge is limited and narrow in scope, and should not be compared with Allah's vast, unlimited and encompassing knowledge — even the particles of objects which the earth disintegrates are well preserved in Allah's infinite knowledge. It then presses the point with an argument drawn from the reader's own body: even the body of a living person is composed of innumerable particles that Allah joined together from different places — whatever a person takes in as food or medicine is derived from different parts of the earth, and all of it forms part of his body. Then why should it be difficult for Him to gather those parts back together after they are disintegrated?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the passage's real astonishment, turning their word back on them: it is astonishing indeed that the disbelievers wonder at Him whose knowledge is so perfect, full, complete and encompassing and whose power is so infinite, and then discount the possibility of Resurrection.

## Ayah 5: the diagnosis

The second "Nay" of the passage lands here, and it moves from what they said to why they said it: "Nay, but they have denied the truth when it has come to them, so they are in a *Marij* state."

Ibn Kathir presents this as Allah explaining the reason behind their disbelief, their rebellion, and their discounting the possibility of what is truly possible. The order matters enormously: the denial came *first*. They did not examine the claim of resurrection and conclude it was false; they denied the truth when it came to them. "This is the state of all those who defy the Truth," writes Ibn Kathir: whatever they say and utter after denying the Truth is utterly false.

**The word *Marij*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it means something mixed up with different elements — and such a thing generally becomes corrupt or spoiled. On that basis Abu Hurairah rendered *marij* as "corrupt," while Ad-Dahhak, Qatadah, Hasan Basri and others took it to mean "in disarray, in a confused state." Ibn Kathir gives the same sense: in disarray, in a confused state, and defying the characteristics of the Truth. Truth has a shape — it is consistent with itself; a *Marij* condition is precisely the absence of that shape.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the confusion concrete. Those who denied the Prophet's ﷺ prophethood were not even consistent in their claims: sometimes they called him a sorcerer, at other times a poet, and yet at other times a soothsayer or an astrologer. They were so confused that they could not extricate themselves from their perplexity. Ibn Kathir points to the same phenomenon in another ayah: "Certainly, you have different ideas. Turned aside therefrom is he who is turned aside" (51:8–9).

That is the passage's quiet proof. Truth is one, so its witnesses agree; a confused state has no single shape, so those in it contradict each other and themselves.

## Living it

**Do not let familiarity blind you.** The deniers' complaint in ayah 2 was that the warner came from among themselves — near, known, one of their own. Nearness is not evidence against something being from Allah.

**Notice the order of belief and argument in yourself.** Ayah 5 places the denial first and the confusion after it. It is worth asking honestly, when we resist something we know to be true, whether our objections are the cause of our resistance or its cover.

**Take the comfort in ayah 4.** The same statement that silences an objector consoles a believer: whatever the earth takes of us is known, and with Allah is a Book preserved. Nothing about us is absent from His knowledge — not the body that disintegrates, and not what is precisely recorded in the Book of decrees.

**And keep this sūrah close.** The Prophet ﷺ recited it in the largest gatherings of his community — the 'Ids and every Friday sermon — and a woman who shared an oven with his household memorized it simply from hearing him. It is a fitting thing for us to hear often too.

passages.title: Sky, earth and rain as proofs of resurrection
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat are Allah's answer to people who discounted the possibility of resurrection. Rather than debate them, He tells them to look — at the sky, at the earth, at what rain does to dead ground.

What holds the passage together is a single line of reasoning that runs from ayah 6 to the last words of ayah 11. Ibn Kathir heads this section **"Allah's Power and Ability over what is Greater than Resurrection."** As he explains it, Allah "notifies the servants of His infinite power, which He demonstrated by creating what is bigger than that which they wondered about and whose possibility they discount." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same connection to what came just before: "After mentioning the confused state of the infidels, Allah draws man's attention to His infinite power which He demonstrated by creating what is bigger than that which they wondered about and whose possibility they discounted." The argument is not from scripture but from scenery. Ibn Kathir will call it, at the end, a sign "that is seen and witnessed."

## Ayah 6 — the roof with no cracks

"Have they not looked at the heaven above them, how We have made it and adorned it, and there are no *Furūj* in it?"

Ibn Kathir explains "adorned it" in one phrase: **"with lamps."** The sky is not merely built, it is decorated — a structure that is also beautiful.

Then the key term. **Furūj**, says Ibn Kathir, means *clefts*, "according to Mujahid"; "others said that Furuj means, rifts, or cracks," and he notes that "all these meanings are close to one another." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the lexical root: *furūj* is "the plural of *farj* which means a crack, or an opening."

What makes this striking is the image of workmanship. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws it out: these ayat direct attention to "the marvels of Allah's creation, the wonderful design in the universe, and to the flawless celestial firmament. If this was made by man there would have been patches, cracks, clefts or rifts. But no one can find any sort of patchwork or stitching in the sky."

Ibn Kathir reinforces the point with the parallel from Sūrah al-Mulk: "Who has created the seven heavens one above another; you can see no fault in the creation of the Most Gracious. Then look again: 'Can you see any rifts?' Then look again and yet again, your sight will return to you in a state of humiliation and worn out" (67:3–4). Ibn Kathir glosses that last phrase as *fatigued* — the eye gives up first, "unable to discover any imperfection or shortcomings." The inspection is invited: look again, and again, and you will exhaust yourself before you find a flaw.

**A precise clarification.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note worth keeping: saying the sky has no cracks "does not negate the existence of doors in the heaven. A door is not referred to as a crack."

## Ayah 7 — the earth beneath, and its anchors

Having sent the eye upward, Allah brings it down. "And the earth! We have spread it out, and set thereon *Rawāsī* standing firm, and We planted in it every lovely (*Bahīj*) pair."

Ibn Kathir takes the three phrases in turn:

- **"We have spread it out"** — meaning, "We made it spacious and spread it out."
- **"and set thereon *Rawāsī* standing firm"** — these, he says, "are the mountains **to save the earth from shaking along with its inhabitants**." The purpose named is not scenery but the safety of the people living there.
- **"and We planted in it every lovely (*Bahīj*) pair"** — meaning "every kind and species of plant, fruit and vegetation," and he cites the related ayah, "And of everything We have created pairs that you may reflect" (51:49). As for ***Bahīj***, Ibn Kathir says it means **"a beautiful scene."**

That last word deserves a pause. Vegetation could have been described only as food. Instead the description is aesthetic: it is *lovely*. Notice too that beauty has now appeared twice in two ayat — the sky is "adorned," the plants are "lovely." Allah's power is not presented here as bare force.

## Ayah 8 — who this evidence actually reaches

"An insight and a Reminder for every servant who turns to Allah in repentance."

This short ayah tells us what all the looking is for. Ibn Kathir: observing the creation of the heavens and the earth "and all the great things that He has placed in them provides insight, proof and a lesson."

But note who receives it: **"every penitent servant who submits in humbleness and repentance to Allah feeling fear, in awe of Him."** That is Ibn Kathir's description of the *munīb*, the servant who turns back. The evidence is public and lying in plain sight; the benefit is not automatic. (A reflection of my own, drawn from this: two people can watch the same rain fall on the same field, and only one of them is reading it as a proof. On the ayah's own terms, what separates them is not eyesight but whether a person is turning back toward Allah.)

Ayah 6 opened with a reproach — *have they not looked* — which suggests that looking, by itself, was never what was missing.

## Ayat 9–10 — the blessed water and what it raises

"And We send down blessed water (rain) from the sky, then We produce therewith *Jannāt* and grain that are reaped. And date palms *Bāsiqāt*, with arranged clusters."

Ibn Kathir works through the details:

- **"blessed water"** — meaning **"beneficial."** The blessing named is the plain good that water does.
- **"*Jannāt*"** — "means special and public parks, gardens, etc."
- **"and grain that are reaped"** — "grains that are harvested for food and for storage for later use."
- **"date palms *Bāsiqāt*"** — meaning **"tall and high,"** and Ibn Kathir reports this explanation from **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and as-Suddī**.
- **"with arranged clusters"** — "producing fruits arranged in clusters."

Read them together and there is a quiet progression. Water falls from above; out of it come gardens, then grain gathered and stored, then palms standing tall with fruit arranged in clusters. The same order and design that ayah 6 pointed to in the sky is here pointed to in a date palm.

## Ayah 11 — the conclusion Allah draws Himself

"A provision for the servants. And We give life therewith to a dead land. Thus will be the Resurrection."

**"A provision for the servants"** — Ibn Kathir says simply, "for (Allah's) creation." Everything just listed is not only a display put up to settle an argument; by Ibn Kathir's own gloss on ayah 9, some of it is grain harvested "for food and for storage for later use."

Then the closing image, which Ibn Kathir describes with real feeling: this is "the land that was barren. However, when rain falls upon it, it is stirred to life; it swells and produces all of the lovely pairs such as flowers and the like — amazing on account of their beauty. All of this comes into existence after the land was without greenery, yet it was stirred back to life and became green."

Dead ground. Water. Life — and not grudging, minimal life, but greenness and flowers and beauty. **"Indeed, this should provide proof of Resurrection after death and disintegration; thus Allah resurrects the dead."** And then Ibn Kathir's sharpest line on the passage: **"This sign of Allah's ability that is seen and witnessed is greater than the denial of those who discount the possibility of Resurrection."** Against a denial stands something visible.

Ibn Kathir closes by lining up three ayat that make the argument from the greater to the lesser explicit:

- "The creation of the heavens and the earth is indeed greater than the creation of mankind" (40:57).
- "Do they not see that Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth, and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, He surely is Able to do all things" (46:33).
- "And among His signs (is this), that you see the earth barren; but when We send down water to it, it is stirred to life and growth. Verily, He Who gives it life, surely is able to give life to the dead. Indeed He is Able to do all things" (41:39).

Read 46:33 slowly: **"and was not wearied by their creation."** The ayah affirms plainly that the creation of the heavens and the earth did not weary Allah — and it draws the conclusion itself: He is therefore able to give life to the dead. Resurrection is not a heavier lift than the sky.

## Living it

**Look up, and mean it.** The passage does not ask for study, only for attention to what is already in front of you — the sky, rain on dry ground, a palm heavy with fruit. Ayah 6 puts its reproach exactly there: *have they not looked*.

**Come as a *munīb*.** Ayah 8 names who this evidence reaches: in Ibn Kathir's words, "every penitent servant who submits in humbleness and repentance to Allah feeling fear, in awe of Him." Ask for that turning back, and the proof already waiting will do its work.

**Let food remind you of the Hereafter.** Ayah 11 calls all of it "a provision for the servants" — for Allah's creation, as Ibn Kathir puts it. The grain and the rain that grew it are, in this passage, part of the same evidence as the flawless heaven.

**Notice the pattern of the argument.** When belief in the Last Day feels thin, the method here is not argument but pointing: the creation of the heavens and the earth "is indeed greater than the creation of mankind" (40:57), and it did not weary Him (46:33). Every time barren land is stirred back to life by rain, that same argument is being made again (41:39).

**And take comfort in the mountains.** Ibn Kathir says they are there "to save the earth from shaking along with its inhabitants." Even the most rigid, silent features of the world were placed with the safety of Allah's servants in view. The One who steadied the ground under you for this life is the One promising you the next.

passages.title: Nations before them who denied the messengers
passages.tafsir:
**A roll-call of ruined nations, and then a single devastating question.** In ayat 12–14 Allah names eight peoples who denied their messengers and were destroyed; in ayah 15 He turns from history to the doubt about being raised again, and answers it with one question: did the first creation tire Me?

The list is not a history lesson. It is evidence. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that in the preceding ayat the disbelievers had rejected two things — the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and the Hereafter — and it reads ayah 12 as saying that resurrection was rejected before them too, by the people of Nūḥ and the rest. So the roll-call answers both charges at once: denial of a messenger is an old, well-documented habit with a consistent ending, and the doubt about a new creation is exposed as confusion rather than argument.

## The passage as consolation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens this section under the heading of consoling the Prophet ﷺ. The rejection recorded in the preceding ayat, it says plainly, perturbed and upset him. So Allah comforts him by narrating the stories of the earlier prophets and their communities. Every community in the past persecuted its own prophet; this was the behaviour pattern of disbelieving nations against their prophets throughout history. The message to him ﷺ is that he should not be disheartened by this behaviour.

The list begins with the longest test of patience named here. Maʿārif notes that Nūḥ (peace be upon him) preached to his people for 950 years, and in response they not only rejected him but subjected him to various hardships. Set beside that, the years of Makkan hostility take on a different scale.

Ibn Kathir reads the same ayat from the other side — as a warning aimed at the deniers rather than a comfort aimed at the Prophet ﷺ. Allah, he writes, warns the disbelievers of Quraysh and reminds them of the punishment and painful torment He sent in this life upon their likes, who disbelieved before them. Both readings live in the same words: the roll-call that steadies a messenger's heart puts his opponents on notice.

## Walking the list

**The people of Nūḥ** (ayah 12). Allah punished them by drowning them in the encompassing flood, which Ibn Kathir describes as touching all the people of the earth.

**The Dwellers of al-Rass** (ayah 12). Ibn Kathir mentions that he has already told their story in Sūrat al-Furqān and does not repeat it here. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives an account worth knowing. Lexically, *rass* in Arabic has several meanings; most prominently it refers to a well that has not been built up with bricks or stones — a bare, dug well. As for who they were, Maʿārif reports from Ḍaḥḥāk and other commentators that they were the remnant of Thamūd who survived the punishment: about four thousand people who escaped because they had reposed faith in Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) and obeyed him. They left their original place and took shelter in Ḥaḍramawt, a city in Yemen. They went to a well and stayed there. Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) was with them and passed away there — which, Maʿārif notes, is why the place is called *Ḥaḍara Mawt*, "death overcame" — and the people settled there permanently.

Then comes the turn in the story. Their descendants took to idol-worship. A prophet was sent to them to preach and reform, and they killed him. The community was annihilated by divine punishment: the very well on which their lives depended was rendered useless, and their buildings and dwellings were left desolate. Maʿārif connects this to the Qur'an's own image — "So, there they are, fallen down on their roofs, and how many a deserted well and well-built castle!" (22:45) — and draws the lesson that for discerning eyes the abandoned well and desolate lofty palaces are sufficient to judge the consequences of one's deeds.

Notice what this account implies: these were the descendants of people who had believed a prophet and been spared with him. A settled and watered life, a place marked by a prophet's own death — none of it transmitted. Faith is not inherited property.

**Thamūd** (ayah 12) — the people of the Prophet Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him), whose story, Maʿārif notes, is repeated several times in the Qur'an.

**ʿĀd** (ayah 13). Maʿārif describes them as proverbial in their size, physical strength and power, as well as in the strength that came to them in the wake of their children. Hūd (peace be upon him) was sent to them, and eventually they were annihilated by the divine punishment of a windstorm. There is a quiet irony in the pairing: the strongest bodies in the list were undone by moving air.

**Firʿawn** (ayah 13). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this is the title of the Egyptian king, notorious for his tyranny. He is the one name in the list that is a single man rather than a people.

**The brethren of Lūṭ** (ayah 13). Ibn Kathir identifies them as the people of Sadūm (Sodom) and the surrounding areas, to whom Lūṭ was sent. Allah shook the earth beneath them and turned their area into a reeking lake — and Ibn Kathir makes the correspondence explicit: as stinking as the disbelief, tyranny and defiance of the truth that they had. The land was made to match the men. Maʿārif glosses "brethren" simply as the community of the Prophet Lūṭ (peace be upon him), whose story is narrated several times in the Qur'an.

**The Dwellers of al-Aykah** (ayah 14). Ibn Kathir identifies them as the nation of Shuʿayb (peace be upon him). Maʿārif explains the name: *aykah* means a dense bush, wood, forest or jungle, and these people resided in such a place. They disobeyed their prophet and were destroyed by divine punishment.

**The people of Tubbaʿ** (ayah 14). Ibn Kathir identifies Tubbaʿ as King of Yemen and refers the reader to his commentary on Sūrat al-Dukhān rather than repeating the story here; Maʿārif adds that Tubbaʿ was the title of the king of Yemen, and likewise points to its treatment under 44:37.

Different nations, different prophets, different punishments — a flood, a windstorm, the earth shaken beneath them, a well made useless. One pattern, stated in the next clause.

## "Each one denied the Messengers"

The heart of ayah 14 is the summary clause: *kullun kadhdhaba al-rusul* — "Everyone of them denied their Messengers." Ibn Kathir points out what is strange about it. Each of these nations belied its own respective Messenger, the one sent to them. Yet Allah says they denied *the Messengers*, plural.

His explanation: whoever denies even one Messenger is as if he has denied all Messengers. He supports this from the Qur'an's own usage — "The people of Nūḥ denied the Messengers" (26:105) — even though only one Messenger was sent to them. And he adds a second reason: indeed, if all the Messengers had been sent to them, they would have disbelieved in them as well. The rejection was never about the particular man. It was a refusal of the whole idea that Allah sends messengers and a human being must obey.

This is worth sitting with, because it is what lets such different nations be gathered into one sentence. Denial is one thing wearing many faces.

## "So My threat took effect"

Then: *fa-ḥaqqa waʿīdi* — "so My threat took effect." Ibn Kathir explains that the promise of torment and punishment which Allah had delivered to them on account of their denial took effect. Note the order in his wording: the promise was delivered first, and only then did it fall due.

Ibn Kathir then applies it directly: therefore, all those who fear suffering the same end should be warned, especially since the latter have denied their Messenger just as the former denied theirs. The pronoun tightens around the listener. The list was never about the past.

## Ayah 15: the question that ends the argument

Having named the pattern, the passage turns to the doubt. *A-fa-ʿayīnā bi-l-khalqi al-awwal* — rendered in the translation as "Were We incapable of creating ˹them˺ the first time?" and by Ibn Kathir as "Were We then tired with the first creation?"

Ibn Kathir puts the meaning as a question the deniers must answer for themselves: did starting the creation bring fatigue to Us, so as to cause doubt in them that repeating the creation was not possible? The objection to resurrection always smuggles in an assumption — that making a thing a second time is harder than making it the first time. Once that assumption is said out loud, it collapses. Nobody watched Allah struggle the first time. There was no strain to run out of.

Ibn Kathir cites the Qur'an's own answer: "And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him" (30:27). And he brings the passage in Sūrah Yā Sīn where a man puts forth a parable and forgets his own creation — "He says: 'Who will give life to these bones after they are rotten and have become dust?' Say: 'He will give life to them Who created them for the first time! And He is the All-Knower of every creation!'" (36:78–79). The man's own body, the arguer's own self, is the standing refutation of the argument.

Note how the second half of ayah 15 frames the objection: *bal hum fī labsin min khalqin jadīd* — "Nay, they are in confused doubt about a new creation." It is not dignified as a claim, a proof, or a theory; it is named as confusion. Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is exact — starting the creation did not tire Us, and repeating it is even easier. The deniers are not holding a considered position. They are in a fog and mistaking it for clarity.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir cites at this point a hadith he identifies as collected in the Ṣaḥīḥ, in which Allah the Exalted said: "Son of Ādam insults Me when he says, 'He will not resurrect me as He created me before!' But surely, originating creation is not easier for Me than reproducing it again."

Two things stand out. First, the word *insults*. Denying the resurrection is not filed as an intellectual mistake; it is filed as an offence against Allah, because of what it says about His power. Second, the reasoning is the same as ayah 15 — the first creation was no easier for Him than the second — which shows how tightly this teaching and this ayah sit together.

## Living it

**Read the list as a mirror, not a museum.** Ibn Kathir's framing is that all those who fear suffering the same end should be warned. The moment we read the roll-call as other people's disasters, we have read it the way the Quraysh did.

**Do not lean on inheritance.** The people of al-Rass, on Maʿārif's account, descended from those who believed Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) and were spared with him — and their descendants ended up killing a prophet. A believing family line is a gift, not a guarantee.

**Take the ruins seriously.** Maʿārif draws the lesson from 22:45 that for discerning eyes, an abandoned well and desolate lofty palaces are enough to judge the consequences of deeds. Empty grandeur is a piece of evidence if you are willing to look at it.

**Check your doubts for the hidden assumption.** Ayah 15 does not argue the resurrection at length. It asks one question that exposes what the doubt was resting on. Most objections to what Allah has told us contain a smuggled premise about His power; naming it is usually the whole answer.

**Notice the order of the warning.** *Fa-ḥaqqa waʿīdi* — the threat took effect, but Ibn Kathir's wording puts the delivering of it first. That is the character of the One who is warning us now.

**And take the consolation as it was given.** If rejection wounded the Prophet ﷺ himself, being wounded by it is no failure of faith. Maʿārif's answer to him ﷺ is the answer to us: this has been the behaviour of disbelieving nations toward their prophets throughout history; do not be disheartened by it.

passages.title: Nearer than the jugular vein; the recording angels
passages.tafsir:
# Surah Qaf, ayat 16–18

These three ayat put two things side by side that we usually keep apart: a nearness so complete that even the unspoken whisper inside you is known, and a record so exact that not a single syllable you utter falls to the ground. Ayah 16 is about what Allah knows of your inside; ayat 17–18 are about what is written of your outside.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maarif ul Quran sets out the linkage. The verses just before this were answering people who denied the possibility of Resurrection and who thought raising the dead was inconceivable. They drew a false analogy between their own finite knowledge and power and the infinite knowledge and power of Allah, and so the perplexity arose in their minds: after we die and disintegrate, our organs torn apart, our bodies reduced to particles of dust and scattered all over the world, how is it possible to gather them together and recompose them back into our original shape?

The reply given earlier was that Allah's knowledge is all-encompassing and He knows every single particle of the universe, so re-collecting those particles is no difficulty for Him. Our passage now elaborates the same subject one step further and inward. It is not only your scattered particles that He knows. He knows every thought that crosses your mind — and the verse explains the reason: **Allah is nearer to you than your jugular vein, on which your very life depends.** Therefore He knows your conditions and circumstances more than you know them yourself. A Lord like that will have no trouble finding your dust.

## "And We know what his self whispers to him" (16)

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah plainly: Allah the Exalted affirms His absolute dominance over mankind, being their Creator and the Knower of everything about them, and He has complete knowledge of all thoughts that cross the mind of man, be they good or evil.

That could be a terrifying sentence on its own. But Ibn Kathir immediately places beside it a hadith he cites as being "in the Sahih," in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Verily, Allah the Exalted has forgiven my Ummah (Muslims) for what they talk (think) to themselves about, as long as they do not utter or implement it."

Hold those two together, because the passage itself does. **Allah knows the whisper — and the whisper is pardoned.** The intrusive thought, the ugly impulse that arrives uninvited, the resentment you refused to feed: known, yes; but forgiven so long as you neither say it nor act on it. And that is exactly the seam on which the passage turns: ayah 16 is knowledge, ayat 17–18 are transcription. Notice how gently the movement is made — you are told first that you are fully known and fully pardoned in your inmost self, and only then that your speech is being written down.

## "Nearer to him than his jugular vein"

**The image.** Maarif ul Quran opens up the word *warid* (plural *awridah*). In the Arabic language these are the veins which supply blood to the entire body. Medically, a distinction is drawn between the veins that emerge from the liver and supply pure blood to the body — thick-walled, and these are what medicine strictly calls *awridah* — and the veins emerging from the heart which supply the subtle vapour of blood, thin-walled, called *shiryan* in Arabic (which actually refers to an artery). The Maarif holds that the word in this ayah need not be taken in the narrow medical sense; since the purport of the verse is to show that Allah has full knowledge of all the thoughts that cross a person's mind, the literal sense of the term seems more appropriate. And in the end the distinction is immaterial: **in both cases the living creature's life depends on it.** If the veins or arteries are cut, they lose their soul and die. That is the whole force of the comparison. The Qur'an did not choose a distant thing to be nearer than; it chose the thing whose failure would end you — and said, *nearer than that*.

**How the scholars understood "nearer".** This is where genuine difference among the commentators lies, and it is worth laying out honestly rather than flattening.

**1. Nearness of knowledge.** Maarif ul Quran reports this as the interpretation of the majority of the commentators, and states that the "closeness" in the verse, by consensus of scholars, refers to nearness in terms of all-encompassing knowledge, not physical closeness. Allah's power and knowledge have so encompassed man from within and without that they are nearer to him than his own jugular vein.

**2. A real but unknowable bond (*ittisal*).** Maarif ul Quran then reports that according to the honourable Sufis, *qurb* here goes beyond nearness in terms of knowledge: it is a special type of *ittisal* — contact or bond or relationship between Allah and His creation — the reality and nature of which is not known to anyone, but which necessarily exists *bila kayf*, "without how," indescribably. As support the Maarif cites the Qur'anic command "and bow down in sajdah, and come closer" (al-Alaq 18, as the Maarif cites it); the report that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The closest that a servant can be to his Lord is when he is in prostration. Therefore, make abundant supplications"; another Tradition reporting that the Prophet ﷺ said, "When My servant performs supererogatory prayers, he attains proximity to Me"; the Prophet's ﷺ words to Sayyidna Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, on the occasion of the migration to Madinah — "Allah is with us" (9:40); and the words of Musa, peace be upon him, to the Children of Israel — "My Lord is with me" (26:62). (The Maarif cites these reports without naming a collection, so take the teaching and leave the attribution.)

This kind of nearness, the Maarif is careful to say, is what man attains through nearness of obligatory and supererogatory works and through his own efforts, and it is reserved exclusively for a believer — such believers are called *awliya'ullah*, the friends of Allah. It is different from the general relationship between Allah and man, whether believer or non-believer. It cannot be perceived by the ordinary sensation of physical sight, but is attained through *farasah* of *iman*, perspicacity through faith. *Tafsir Mazhari* interprets *qurb* and *ittisal* in this verse in the same sense. The Maarif quotes Maulana Rumi's versification of the idea: "The Lord of the people has a special contact with the people which is beyond one's perception and has no other example."

**3. The angels.** Ibn Kathir takes a third way, which Maarif ul Quran notes as distinct from the other two: the pronoun "We" does not refer to the Being of Allah but to **His angels**, who are with man all the time and who know his soul so closely that man himself is not so well aware of it. Ibn Kathir's own reasoning is worth following, because it is as much about how we read Allah's speech as it is about angels:

- Those who explained "We" in the ayah to mean "Our knowledge" did so to avoid falling into the idea of incarnation or indwelling. Ibn Kathir agrees that these two creeds are false according to the consensus of Muslims — Allah is praised and glorified, far hallowed beyond what they ascribe to Him. But, he argues, the words of this ayah do not need that explanation.
- Why not? Because **Allah did not say, "and I am closer to him than his jugular vein."** He said, "**We** are nearer to him than his jugular vein" — just as He said in the case of dying persons, "But We are nearer to him than you, but you see not" (56:85), in reference to His angels who take the souls.
- He gives a further parallel: "Verily, We, it is We Who have sent down the Dhikr and surely, We will guard it" (15:9) — and the angels brought down the revelation, the Qur'an, by the leave of Allah. So a "We" in Allah's speech may be fulfilled through His angels acting by His leave.
- Therefore, Ibn Kathir concludes, the angels are closer to man than his own jugular vein, by the power and leave of Allah. Consequently the angel touches mankind just as the devil touches them, for the devil is as close to them as the blood that runs in their veins — as Allah's Prophet ﷺ, who is truthful and was told the truth, told us.

**Creed, plainly.** All three readings share one thing, and you should hold onto it: none of them makes Allah a body located inside yours. The two commentaries are explicit that incarnation and indwelling are false by the consensus of Muslims, and that Allah is far hallowed above what such people ascribe to Him. Affirm what He affirmed of Himself — that He is nearer to you than your jugular vein — without likening it to the nearness of created things and without emptying the words of meaning. And where the scholars themselves differed, as here, take the difference as depth rather than as a problem you must settle.

## The two receivers (17)

**"When the two receivers receive."** *Idh yatalaqqa al-mutalaqqiyan.* Maarif ul Quran traces the verb *yatalaqqa* to the infinitive *talaqqi*, which denotes to take, to accept, to receive, to learn — as in the verse, "Thereafter Adam received a few words from his Lord" (2:37). *Al-mutalaqqiyani* is the dual, and it refers to the two angels that accompany every human being all the time to receive and record the deeds of mankind. The verb is not "watch" or "hear" but *receive*: what you do is handed over, taken in, and kept.

**"One sitting on the right and one on the left."** Ibn Kathir glosses "sitting" as **ready to note**. Maarif ul Quran opens the word *qa'id* further. In one usage the word means a person who is actually sitting; but it is also used in the general sense of one who accompanies someone — whether sitting, standing, or moving around. The word is used in this verse to describe the two angels precisely because they accompany human beings all the time and in every state: sitting or standing, moving or sleeping. The Maarif adds that the angels move out only when a person uncovers himself to answer the call of nature or for intimacy with his spouse; but Allah has equipped them with a special innate sensing device, so that they still become aware of sins committed in their absence.

Their division of labour: **the angel sitting on the right records one's good actions, and the one on the left, his bad actions.**

**Mercy built into the system.** Maarif ul Quran relays that Ibn Kathir states, according to the narration of Ahnaf Ibn Qais, that the angel sitting on the right records the good deeds and is also the supervisor over the angel on the left. If a person commits a sin, the angel on the right says to the one on the left, "Do not write it yet; give him a chance; maybe he will repent; if he does, then let it go; otherwise record it in your record of deeds." (Ibn-Abi Haim transmitted it, as the Maarif names it.) The recording apparatus, in other words, is not a hostile machine. There is a pause built into it, and the pause is on the side of your repentance.

**Hasan Basri's address.** Maarif ul Quran records that Hasan Basri, may Allah have mercy on him, recited the phrase "seated one on the right, and one on the left" and said:

> "O son of Adam! Your record of deeds has been spread, and two honorable angels have been appointed. One on your right side and the other on your left. The one on your right side records your good deeds, and the one on your left records your evil deeds and sins. Focus on this reality, and do what you desire, increase it or decrease it. When you die, your record of deeds will be folded, and put around your neck. It will go with you in the grave, and remain there. When you will rise from your grave on the Day of Judgment, Allah will say: 'And every human's (deeds determining his) fate We have tied up to his neck, and We shall bring forth for him, on the day of Resurrection, a book he will receive wide open. Read your book. This day you yourself are enough to take your own account.'" (Surah Bani Isra'il 13, 14)

Hasan Basri then swore an oath and said that the Supreme Being has done a great justice in that He has appointed you to take account of your own actions. Maarif ul Quran attributes this to Ibn Kathir.

Maarif ul Quran adds a note against literalism here: obviously the book or ledger of deeds would not be made up of mundane paper, so there need be no difficulty in understanding how it goes with a person into the grave and remains with him until the Day of Resurrection. It is a transcendental reality, the actual nature of which is known only to Allah.

## "Not a word does he utter" (18)

*Ma yalfizu min qawlin illa ladayhi raqibun 'atid.* Maarif ul Quran renders it: "Not a single word is uttered by one, but there is a watcher near him, ready to record" — meaning there is always a supervising angel, the scribe, whose responsibility is to record any word that the human utters or speaks. Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase the same way: there is a scribe whose job is to record it, **leaving no word or movement unrecorded**. Ibn Kathir sets alongside it: "But verily, over you are appointed angels to watch you, Kiraman (honorable) Katibin writing down your deeds, they know all that you do" (82:10–12).

**How much is written?** Here the early authorities differed:

- **Hasan Basri and Qatadah**, may Allah have mercy on them: this angel records **every single word** — whether or not it is sinful or rewardable.
- **Ibn Abbas**, may Allah be pleased with him: only those utterances are recorded that are sinful or rewardable.
- **Ibn Kathir's preference:** having quoted both views, he preferred the first, on the basis of the general words of the verse that every utterance is recorded. He calls it the apparent meaning of the ayah.
- **A reconciliation**, reported by Maarif ul Quran from another narration of Sayyidna Abu Talhah from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them: in the first instance every utterance is recorded, whether or not it is sinful or rewardable; then once a week, on Thursdays, the angels review the recorded utterances and retain only those that are sinful or rewardable, good or bad, while the rest are discounted. The Maarif connects this to the Qur'an's words: "Allah wipes off what He wills and affirms what He wills. And with Him is the Mother Book" (Ar-Ra'd 39).

**The hadith that made Alqamah hold his tongue.** Imam Ahmad recorded that Bilal bin Al-Harith Al-Muzani, may Allah be pleased with him, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Verily, a man might utter a word that pleases Allah the Exalted, unaware of how highly it will be regarded, and on its account Allah the Exalted and Most Honored decrees His pleasure of him until the Day he meets Him. A man might indeed utter a word that angers Allah the Exalted, unaware of how dreadful it will be and on its account Allah the Exalted decrees for him His anger until the Day he meets Him."

Ibn Kathir notes that At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah also collected this hadith, that At-Tirmidhi said "Hasan Sahih," and that there is a hadith similar to this in the Sahih. And Alqamah, who narrated it from Bilal bin Al-Harith, used to say: **"How many words did I not utter because of this hadith."**

That line is the passage's practical residue. Not "how many sins did I avoid" — how many *words*. The danger the ayah identifies is not only the deliberate lie or the calculated slander; it is the sentence you throw out without weighing it, the one you would not think worth remembering by dinnertime, which is written and which may fix Allah's pleasure or His anger upon you until you meet Him. Notice what the hadith stresses twice: the speaker is *unaware* of what his word will amount to. You do not get to judge the weight of your own speech. That assessment happens elsewhere.

## Living it

**Be at ease about the whisper.** What passes through you unbidden and unspoken is known to Allah, and this Ummah has been forgiven for what they talk to themselves about so long as they do not utter or act on it. Do not build a spiritual crisis out of a thought.

**Be careful at the mouth.** The line between the pardoned and the recorded is the lips. Ayah 18 puts a scribe at that line, ready. The most useful habit this passage can leave you with is a half-second of hesitation before speech — Alqamah's habit.

**Take the right-hand angel's pause seriously.** If the narration of Ahnaf Ibn Qais is a window into how the record is kept, then repentance offered soon after a sin can meet it before the ink dries. Delay is the only thing that hardens it.

**And read the nearness as invitation, not only as surveillance.** The Maarif's second reading is that the way to draw closer is exactly the way you already know: the obligatory works, then the supererogatory ones — and the closest a servant can be to his Lord is when he is in prostration, so make abundant supplications there.

So the passage leaves you held between two facts about yourself. Two angels are at your shoulders, receiving and keeping the file that will be folded and hung around your neck. And the One who is nearer to you than your jugular vein already knows what is in it — including everything in you that never reached your tongue at all.

passages.title: Death throes, the Trumpet, and the record produced
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat follow one human being through the journey nobody is exempt from: the last breath, the blast of the Trumpet, the march to the place of gathering, the veil removed, and the record produced. What binds them is that they are one continuous statement about being watched and then being shown. Just before this passage Allah has said that He knows what a man's self whispers to him, that two angels sit receiving and recording on the right and the left, and that "there is a watcher by him ready" (ayah 18). Ayat 19–23 carry that recording forward to the moment it is produced.

## Ayah 19 — the daze of death, arriving with the truth

**سَكْرَةُ الْمَوْتِ — the daze of death.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the phrase *sakrat-ul-mawt* "denotes the agony and the stupor or daze of death that a dying person experiences." Death is not presented here as an idea to be debated but as something that physically overtakes a person.

**"with the truth" — بِالْحَقِّ.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, notes that in this prepositional phrase the small word *bāʾ* ("with") passes the action of the verb on to an object: the pangs of death do not merely arrive, they *bring something with them* — "things that are true and real which none can escape or avoid." Ibn Kathir reads it the same way, putting it in Allah's voice: "O mankind! This is the stupor of death that has come in truth; now, I have brought forth to you the certainty that you were disputing." Everything a person argued about stops being a matter of opinion at that moment. Death is the courier that delivers the certainty.

**تَحِيدُ — what you kept swerving from.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces this verb to the root *ḥayd*, which "denotes to incline; to turn aside or escape from a place; to avoid or shun it; and to acknowledge." It is the word for veering off, dodging, keeping one's eyes elsewhere. Ibn Kathir gives the closing phrase two possible meanings, and both are worth holding: first, "what you have been trying to avert, escape and flee from has come to you and resided in your home"; second, "you had no way of escaping or averting this end." One is about arrival, the other about futility.

**Fearing death is not a sin.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a point of unusual tenderness here. This ayah, it says, apparently addresses the entire mankind. "Every man is naturally afraid or scared of, or alarmed and terrified by, the thought of death. Life is dear to him and death is a calamity for him. As a result, he makes plans to run away from death. This is from Sharʿi point of view not wrong or a sin." Wanting to live is not a defect of faith. The point of the ayah is only that the plan cannot finally succeed: "you will have neither a shelter nor a refuge nor a sanctuary nor an asylum from it."

**The fox and its debt.** Ibn Kathir cites a hadith collected by At-Tabarani in *Al-Muʿjam Al-Kabir* from Samurah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The parable of whoever tries to avoid death is that of a fox that had a debt to pay to the earth. The fox went away and when he became tired and the time to sleep overtook him, he entered his den. The earth said to him, 'O fox! Pay my debt!' The fox went out howling and continued until his neck was cut off, (i.e.,) he died." Ibn Kathir draws the lesson plainly: just as the fox had no way of escaping or avoiding the earth, man has no way of avoiding death. All the running achieved was exhaustion; the claim was still waiting when he stopped.

**Abu Bakr's correction at his own deathbed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, from Abu Bakr Ibn al-Anbari with his own transmitting authorities from Masruq, that when the signs of death appeared on Sayyidnā Abu Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, ʿA'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, was called. Seeing her father's condition, she spontaneously recited a line of verse: "When the soul one day will be uneasy and the breast thereby will become narrow." Her father heard it and said: "You recited this verse inappropriately; why did you not recite the Qur'anic verse — *And the daze of death has come with truth. That is what you tried to escape*." Even in his last hours he was teaching: at the deathbed, take the words Allah gave you.

**The Prophet ﷺ in the same state.** Ibn Kathir reports that in the Sahih, the Prophet ﷺ said, while wiping sweat from his face when the stupor of death overcame him: "Glory be to Allah! Verily, death has its stupor." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same moment with the detail that when he ﷺ faced this state he would put his hand in the water and wipe it over his blessed face, reciting, "There is no god but Allah; indeed death has its pangs." The Prophet ﷺ himself was not spared the throes of death. A dying believer's struggle is the same road he walked.

## Ayah 20 — the Trumpet and the Day of the threat

**وَنُفِخَ فِي الصُّورِ.** Ibn Kathir notes that he has already discussed elsewhere the blowing of the Trumpet, the fear that follows it, the death of everything and then the resurrection — all of it occurring on the Day of Resurrection. Here the blast is named in a single clause, as if to say that after a person's private death comes the public one.

**يَوْمُ الْوَعِيدِ.** Ibn Kathir renders the phrase "that will be the Day of the threat"; the translation given with the ayah reads "This is the Day ˹you were˺ warned." (Later in this same surah, at ayah 28 — beyond our passage — Ibn Kathir records Allah saying to those disputing before Him, "I had already in advance sent you the threat," which Ibn Kathir explains as: "I have given you sufficient proof by the words of the Messengers, and I have sent down the Divine Books; the evidences, signs and proofs have thus been established against you.")

**The angel with the Trumpet already at his lips.** Ibn Kathir recalls a hadith in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "How can I feel comfort while the angel responsible for the Trumpet has placed the Trumpet to his mouth and lowered his forehead awaiting when he will be commanded (by Allah to blow in it)?" They said, "O Allah's Messenger, what should we say?" He ﷺ said: "Say, *Ḥasbunā Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl* — Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs." And the Companions repeated it. (Ibn Kathir relates this teaching here without naming the collection it comes from, so it is given as he gives it.)

That exchange is one of the most practical things in the passage. The Prophet ﷺ did not answer their fear by softening the picture; he answered it by giving them a sentence to say. Neither denial nor despair — the matter entrusted to Allah.

## Ayah 21 — driven, and witnessed against

**سَائِق — the driver.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the literal picture: *sāʾiq* "denotes a person who remains behind a herd of animals or behind a group of people and drives them to a particular place." He is behind, not in front — this is not a guide to be followed but a driver at one's back.

**شَهِيد — the witness.** *Shahīd*, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "refers to a witness." Ibn Kathir explains the ayah as "an angel to drive him to the gathering place and an angel to bear witness against him with regards to his deeds," and says this is the apparent meaning of this honourable ayah and the meaning Ibn Jarir preferred. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd placed the same interpretation on the two names.

Both sources record that ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him, recited this ayah while delivering a sermon and said: "A *Sāʾiq* to drive every person to Allah the Exalted, and a *Shahid* to witness against him what he has done." Ibn Kathir additionally names the transmission: it was narrated from Yahya bin Rafiʿ, the freed servant of Thaqif, that he heard ʿUthman say it.

**Where the scholars differed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the views out honestly. That the *sāʾiq* is an angel is settled "by the consensus of traditions." About the *shahīd* there is genuine difference among the scholars of tafsir:

- that he too is an angel — so that there are two angels, one driving the people to the gathering place and one bearing witness when their deeds are presented; this is what Ibn Kathir considers the apparent sense of the words, what Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd held, and what Ibn Jarir preferred;
- that the two are the "honourable scribes" who accompanied the person on his right and left throughout life, recording his deeds;
- that they are some other angels besides these;
- that the *shahīd* refers to the person's own action;
- that the *shahīd* is the man himself.

If the second view is right, the passage becomes tighter still: the very pair who sat beside a person unnoticed for a lifetime are the pair who walk him to judgement.

**Note the "every".** *Kullu nafs* — the ayah speaks of every person, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it in the singular: "With every man there will be a *Sāʾiq* and a *Shahid*." The escort is not shared.

## Ayah 22 — the covering removed

**"You were heedless of this."** Ibn Kathir explains the heedlessness here as heedlessness "of this Day" — not ignorance so much as inattention, living as though the Day were not coming. Then: *fa-kashafnā ʿanka ghiṭāʾak*, "Now We have removed from you, your covering."

**فَبَصَرُكَ الْيَوْمَ حَدِيدٌ — "sharp is your sight this Day."** Ibn Kathir glosses it simply: "your sight is now clear and strong."

**Who is being addressed?** The translation of the ayah reproduced in Ibn Kathir's text carries the parenthetical "(It will be said to the sinners)", yet Ibn Kathir's own comment on the words is that this address "is directed at humanity." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the difference of opinion openly and gives the preferred position: "the preferred opinion is that Allah addresses mankind in general. This includes the believers, the unbelievers, the pious and the wicked," noting that Ibn Jarir, Ibn Kathir and others adopted this interpretation.

**Asleep, then awake.** The analogy Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws is the heart of this ayah: this world is like the dream-world and the Hereafter is like the state of wakefulness. While a man is in the dream-world his eyes are closed and he cannot perceive, by his physical organs of sight, the stark realities of the next world; when those physical organs of sight close, the dream-world ends, wakefulness begins, and he is able to discern those realities. The change the analogy describes is in the sleeper, not in what is there to be seen. Hence the aphorism the scholars formulated: *al-nāsu niyāmun fa-idhā mātū intabahū* — "People are sleeping in this world; when they die, they will wake up."

**But clear sight can come too late.** Ibn Kathir is careful here: everyone, including the disbelievers, will have clear sight on the Day of Resurrection — yet having sight will not be helpful to the disbelievers on that Day. He cites Allah's words, "How clearly will they see and hear, the Day when they will appear before Us!" (19:38), and the scene of the criminals hanging their heads before their Lord: "Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back, that we will do righteous good deeds. Verily, we now believe with certainty" (32:12). Certainty arrives for everybody. Its worth depends entirely on when it arrives.

## Ayah 23 — the record, ready

**"Here is what I have, ready."** Ibn Kathir explains that the scribe angel, entrusted with recording the deeds of mankind, will testify against the person about the deeds he did on the Day of Resurrection, saying *hādhā mā ladayya ʿatīd* — "here it is prepared and completed without addition or deletion." Nothing has been slipped in; nothing has been quietly removed.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies *qarīn* ("companion") as the recording angel that accompanies man all the time, and reads the two ayat together: of the two scribes named in the preceding ayah, one — the *Sāʾiq* — will drive the people to the gathering place, and the second — the *Shahid* — will carry the record of deeds and, on reaching the plain of *Ḥashr*, will say, "This is what I have with me, ready." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Ibn Jarir, in his tafsir, states that the word *qarīn* comprehends both angels, the *Sāʾiq* and the *Shahid*.

**One word closes the circle.** The word that ends ayah 23 is *ʿatīd*, "ready" — the same word that ends ayah 18, *raqībun ʿatīd*, "a watcher by him ready." Ready to write; ready to present.

*(A note to prevent confusion as you read on: in ayah 27 the word* qarīn *appears again, and there Ibn Kathir reports, from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and several others, that it refers to the devil entrusted to every man, who will disown him. The companion who hands over the record in ayah 23 and the companion who blames the man in ayah 27 are not the same companion.)*

## Living it

**Watch the tongue, because the record is being written now.** Commenting on ayah 18, just before this passage, Ibn Kathir records that Imam Ahmad reported from Bilal bin al-Harith al-Muzani that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Verily, a man might utter a word that pleases Allah the Exalted, unaware of how highly it will be regarded, and on its account Allah decrees His pleasure of him until the Day he meets Him. A man might indeed utter a word that angers Allah the Exalted, unaware of how dreadful it will be, and on its account Allah decrees for him His anger until the Day he meets Him." Ibn Kathir notes that Alqamah used to say, "How many words did I not utter because of the hadith that Bilal bin al-Harith narrated," and that At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah collected it, At-Tirmidhi saying "Hasan Sahih." The record produced in ayah 23 is being compiled in today's conversations.

**Take the mercy alongside the warning.** In the same passage Ibn Kathir cites the Prophet ﷺ, in the Sahih: "Verily, Allah the Exalted has forgiven my Ummah for what they talk to themselves about, as long as they do not utter or implement it." The two receiving angels are real, and Ibn Kathir says the scribe records every word that is spoken — but what stays inside, unspoken and unacted, this Ummah has been forgiven.

**Do not build your life on escaping.** Fearing death is natural and not a sin, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says. Arranging your life as though the escape could actually be engineered is the fox's mistake.

**Wake before you are woken.** If this world is the dream and the Hereafter the waking, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's analogy has it, then faith now is the work of discerning, while the eyes are still closed, what will be plain when they open. And when the fear of that Day rises, the Prophet ﷺ has already handed you the words: *Ḥasbunā Allāhu wa niʿma al-wakīl* — Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs.

passages.title: Cast into Hell and the devil's disowning
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat are the closing scene of a courtroom. The record has just been produced — in ayah 23 the recording angel says, "Here is (his record) ready with me!" — and now the verdict is spoken, the accused tries to shift the blame onto the devil who shadowed him all his life, the devil throws it straight back, and Allah silences them both. What holds the passage together is a single question: on that Day, whose fault was it? The answer is given from three directions — the charge sheet (24–26), the failed excuse (27–29), and finally the Fire itself, still hungry (30).

## The verdict: "Throw him in" (ayah 24)

Ibn Kathir explains that the scribe angel entrusted with recording the deeds of mankind will testify against the person about the deeds he or she did on the Day of Resurrection, presenting a record "prepared and completed without addition or deletion." There is no dispute over the evidence. It is at this point — when, as Ibn Kathir puts it, Allah the Exalted will judge the creation with fairness — that the command comes: **alqiyā fī jahannama** — "Both of you throw into Hell."

A small grammatical detail carries the whole scene. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the verb **alqiyā** is grammatically *dual* in number — that is, addressed to two persons: not "throw" to one, nor "throw" to a crowd, but a command addressed to exactly two. Who are the two? It appears, Ibn Kathir says, that Allah will say these words to the **Sāʾiq** and the **Shahīd** angels — the Sāʾiq drove him to the grounds where the Reckoning is held, and the Shahīd testified. The same two who escorted him in are the two ordered to cast him out. Ibn Kathir notes that some other scholars explain it differently, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān repeats that caveat, so this is offered as the apparent meaning rather than a settled one.

## The charge sheet (ayat 24–26)

The one being cast in is described with a series of words, each opening a different door onto the same character.

**Kaffār ʿanīd — "stubborn disbeliever."** Ibn Kathir glosses this as one "whose disbelief and denial of truth was horrendous, who used to stubbornly reject the truth, knowingly contradicting it with falsehood." Note the word *knowingly*. This is not the confusion of someone who never heard, but the hardness of someone who saw and dug in.

**Mannāʿ lil-khayr — "hinderer of good."** Ibn Kathir reads this not merely as blocking others from good, but as a life emptied of it: "he did not fulfill the duties he was ordered, nor was he dutiful, keeping ties to kith and kin nor giving charity." Three concrete things are named — the obligations Allah placed on him, the bonds of family, and the giving of wealth. Withholding good is not an abstract vice; it has a shape you could have watched from across the street.

**Muʿtad — "transgressor."** Ibn Kathir explains it as one who transgresses the limits in spending. Qatādah widened it: "He is a transgressor in his speech, behavior and affairs." So the two glosses sit side by side — a man who broke the boundaries with his money, and a man who broke them with everything.

**Murīb — "doubter."** This word is worth pausing on, because Ibn Kathir gives it two faces at once: "he doubts and raises doubts in those who scrutinize his behavior." Both are there — the doubt he carries, and the doubt he spreads. His unsettledness is contagious; when people look closely at how he lives, they come away less sure, not more.

**Alladhī jaʿala maʿa Allāhi ilāhan ākhar — "who set up another god with Allah"** (ayah 26). Ibn Kathir: "he associated others with Allah and worshipped others besides Him." This is the root beneath the branches. And then the command is repeated with a chilling narrowing: the first order was to throw *every* stubborn disbeliever into Hell — a whole category; now it is **fa-alqiyāhu**, "then both of you cast **him** in the severe torment" — one particular person, one pronoun, no crowd to hide inside.

### From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir cites here a hadith recorded by **Imam Ahmad**, that Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A neck from the Fire will appear and will speak saying, 'Today, I have been entrusted with three: Every obstinate tyrant, everyone who ascribed another god with Allah, and he who took a life without right.' The neck will then close in on them and throw them in the midst of Jahannam." Two of the three named there — the obstinate one and the one who ascribed another god with Allah — are precisely the descriptions of ayat 24 and 26.

## The devil disowns his man (ayah 27)

Now the scene turns. **Qāla qarīnuh** — "his companion will say."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the word: **qarīn** literally denotes a companion, that is, one who accompanies or associates with another. That is why the same word in the preceding ayah referred to the two angels that accompany human beings and record their deeds. But just as there are two angels in the company of man, there is a devil entrusted to every man, who calls him towards the commission of sins and thus leads him astray — and *this* is the qarīn meant in ayah 27. Ibn Kathir reports that this is the explanation of ʿAbdullāh bin ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah and several others.

What makes the moment so bitter is what precedes it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sketches it: when it will be ordered that the person be thrown into Hell, it seems that he will say that the devil had led him astray, otherwise he would have done righteous deeds. Ibn Kathir puts the words in his mouth: "O, Lord! This devil has misguided me away from the Remembrance after it came to me." A lifetime of following, and at the first moment of consequence he turns on his companion.

And the companion turns on him faster. **Rabbanā mā aṭghaytuh** — "Our Lord! I did not push him to transgression" — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, "I did not lead him astray." **Wa lākin kāna fī ḍalālin baʿīd** — "but he was himself in error far astray": he himself was misguided, accepting falsehood and stubborn to the truth. Notice that the devil does not claim the man was innocent; he claims the man was already lost. The defence and the prosecution agree on everything except whom to blame.

Ibn Kathir sets alongside this the speech of Shayṭān in Sūrah Ibrāhīm, when the matter has been decided: "Verily, Allah promised you a promise of truth. And I too promised you, but I betrayed you. I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me. So blame me not, but blame yourselves" (14:22). That is the theological heart of the whole exchange. The devil's power was never force. It was invitation — he called, and the response was the man's own.

## "Do not dispute before Me" (ayat 28–29)

Allah cuts through the argument: **lā takhtaṣimū ladayya** — "Dispute not in front of Me." Ibn Kathir explains that the Lord, the Exalted and Most Honored, will say this to the man and his devil companion, who will be disputing before Him. The quarrel is not settled by hearing more of it; it is ended.

Why? **Wa qad qaddamtu ilaykum bil-waʿīd** — "I had already in advance sent you the threat." Ibn Kathir unpacks it: "I have given you sufficient proof by the words of the Messengers, and I have sent down the Divine Books; the evidences, signs and proofs have thus been established against you." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same explanation — the words of the past Messengers, the Divine Books, the proofs established — and adds the sting: "your flimsy excuses, arguments and disputes will not work today." The warning was not sprung on anyone at the last moment; that is exactly what *qaddamtu*, "I put it forward, in advance," means. Every excuse offered in that courtroom is an excuse that was answered before the trial began.

**Mā yubaddalu al-qawlu ladayya** — "The Sentence that comes from Me cannot be changed." Mujāhid explained this simply: "I have made My decision." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān expands it: the decision will certainly be implemented, and it will never be changed.

Then the ayah closes on something we might not expect at the end of a sentence of condemnation: **wa mā anā bi-ẓallāmin lil-ʿabīd** — "and I am not unjust to the servants." Ibn Kathir renders the meaning: "I will not punish anyone, except on account of their sins after the proof has been established against them." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it "an absolutely fair and just decision." Two conditions are stated there, and both must hold: a person is punished *for his own sins*, and only *after* the proof has been established against him. The passage that began with a command to throw a man into the Fire ends by insisting that no one is wronged. Justice is not the opposite of this severity — it is its foundation.

## "Are you full?" (ayah 30)

The final ayah widens the camera from one man to the whole Fire. **Yawma naqūlu li-jahannama hal imtalaʾti** — "On the Day when We will say to Hell: 'Are you filled?'" **Wa taqūlu hal min mazīd** — "It will say: 'Are there any more?'"

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah, the Most Honored, has promised Hell that it will have its fill from the Jinns and mankind; He will decide who will be thrown into the Fire, and she will keep saying, "Are there any more," or, "Are there any more whom You will provide me with?" He states that this is the apparent meaning of the ayah, and that it is supported by several hadiths.

He then cites them. **Imam Ahmad** recorded that Anas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The people will be thrown into Jahannam and it will say, 'Are there any more?' Until the Mighty Lord puts His Foot over it and its corners will be collected together and it will say, 'Enough, enough by Your grace and compassion!' There will be sufficient empty space in Paradise until Allah creates another creation and He, the Exalted, makes them dwell in the empty parts of Paradise." Ibn Kathir notes that **Muslim** also collected this hadith. **Al-Bukhari** recorded that Abū Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said the same in shorter form: "Jahannam will be asked, 'Are you full?' and it will say, 'Are there any more?' Until the Lord, the Blessed and Most Honored, puts His Foot over it and it will say: 'Enough! Enough!'"

**Al-Bukhari** also recorded that Abū Hurayrah said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Paradise and the Fire quarreled. The Fire said, 'I have been favored with the arrogant people and tyrants.' Paradise said, 'What is wrong with me that only the poor and humble people enter me?' Allah the Exalted and Most Honored said to Paradise, 'You are My mercy, with which I grant mercy to those whom I will among My servants.' He said to Hell, 'You are My punishment which I inflict upon whom I wish from My servants, and I shall fill both of you.'" As for Hellfire, the hadith continues, it will not have its fill until Allah puts His Foot over it and she will say, "Enough! Enough!" — she will become full and its sides will come close to each other — "and Allah the Exalted and Most Honored shall not be unjust to any one of His creatures." As for Paradise, Allah the Exalted and Most Honored will create another creation to fill it.

That last clause is the same note ayah 29 ended on. Even the hadith about the filling of Hell pauses to say that no creature of His is wronged. The scene is severe, and in the same breath it is just.

## Living it

The passage is not describing a stranger. Read the descriptions of ayat 24–26 again as questions rather than as a portrait: Do I know something is true and dig in against it anyway? Are the duties I was commanded actually done — the ties of kith and kin kept, the charity given? Do I keep to limits in what I spend? Does someone who scrutinizes my life come away steadier in faith, or less sure?

And the deepest lesson is in ayah 27. The excuse that feels so natural — *he made me do it, the temptation was too strong* — is voiced on that Day and collapses on the spot, refuted by the tempter himself: "I did not push him to transgression." The devil calls; he does not compel — "I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me." So the honest response to a whispering is never to negotiate with the whisperer, and never to store up a defence for later. There is no defence later. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says of ayah 28: the flimsy excuses, arguments and disputes will not work that day.

Yet the passage does not leave us in despair. The very sentence that seals the punishment is the sentence that guarantees Allah's justice — no one is punished except on account of his own sins, and only after the proof has been established against him. That the truth has reached you is the warning. That it reached you *in advance* is the mercy.

passages.title: Paradise brought near to the mindful
passages.tafsir:
