These five ayat are the other half of a picture. Just before them, in ayah 30, Hell is asked whether it is full and answers, "Are there any more?" — a mouth that never closes. Now the camera turns, and Paradise is brought forward to meet the people who had *taqwa*. What holds ayat 31–35 together is a single movement: the Garden draws near (31), a voice identifies exactly who it is for (32–33), the invitation is given (34), and the reward is described as open-ended, more than the people of Paradise could have thought to ask for (35).

## The Garden comes to them

**"And Paradise will be brought near to the righteous, not far" (ayah 31).** The Qur'an's word here is *uzlifat*. Ibn Kathir reports from Qatadah, Abu Malik and As-Suddi that it means Paradise will be brought close and near to the pious. Notice the direction of travel in the phrasing: they are not described as climbing toward it; it is brought toward them. On the day when everything else is terror, the reward is already standing at their side.

*Ghayra baʿīd* — "not far." Ibn Kathir attaches this to the timing as well as the place: this will occur on the Day of Resurrection, "which is not far off. Surely that Day will come to pass and all that is bound to come, is near." The distance you feel between yourself and the Hereafter is an illusion of the present moment. Everything guaranteed to arrive is, by definition, close.

**Who are the *muttaqīn*?** They are, in Ibn Kathir's rendering, "those who had *taqwa*" — the pious. The ayat that follow do not leave this abstract; they spell it out in four terms.

## Four words that describe a life

**Awwāb (ayah 32) — the one who keeps coming back.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *awwāb* refers to the person who turns to Allah, and here specifically who turns to Him in repentance from sins. It records that ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, al-Shaʿbi and Mujahid said *awwāb* is the one who **recalls his sins in loneliness, in private and in secret, and seeks Allah's forgiveness** — not the public penitent, but the man alone with his memory. ʿUbaid ibn ʿUmair said the *awwāb* is one who seeks Allah's forgiveness of his sins in every sitting, and he further said that we are advised to recite this invocation:

> سُبْحَانَ اللهِ وَبِحَمْدِهِ، اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْتَغْفِرُكَ مِمَّا أَصَبْتُ فِي مَجْلِسِي هٰذَا
>
> "Pure is Allah and praise be to Him. O Allah, I seek Your forgiveness of the evil that I might have committed in this sitting."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes that in a Prophetic tradition we are advised to recite the following when a gathering disperses, and that Allah will forgive the sins that might have been committed in that session:

> سُبْحَانَكَ اللَّهُمَّ وَبِحَمْدِكَ، لَا إِلٰهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ، أَسْتَغْفِرُكَ وَأَتُوبُ إِلَيْكَ
>
> "Pure are You, O Allah, and praise be to You. There is no god but You. I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in penitence."

Ibn Kathir's gloss adds the crucial condition: those returning are the ones who go back to Allah in sincere repentance **"intending not to repeat sin."** Repentance is not a mood; it carries a decision inside it.

**Hafīz (ayah 32) — the one who keeps guard.** Ibn Kathir gives it as those "who preserve their covenant with Allah and do not break or betray it." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports two definitions from Ibn ʿAbbas: the *hafīz* is one who **remembers his sins**, so that he may return to Allah in penitence and make amends; and in another report from him, one who **guards the command of Allah** — who remembers his covenant with Allah and does not break or betray it.

Put the pair together and you have a complete spiritual posture. *Awwāb* is the movement back after failure; *hafīz* is the vigilance that limits failure in the first place. Neither alone is enough. A person who returns but never guards will spend his life in the same circle; a person who guards but never returns has no doorway when he slips.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites Qurtubi for a narration from Abu Hurayrah, who reports from the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever performs four rakʿat of Ishraq prayer early in the day is *awwāb* and *hafīz*." It is worth pausing on how modest that is: two titles the Qur'an attaches to the inheritors of Paradise, attached by the Prophet ﷺ to a short prayer offered early in the day, before the day has had a chance to pull you away.

**"Who feared Ar-Rahman unseen" (ayah 33)** — rendered in the translation as being "in awe of the Most Compassionate without seeing Him."

*Bi'l-ghayb* — "unseen," "in the unseen." Ibn Kathir reads it of the servant: one "who feared Allah in secret when only Allah the Exalted and Most Honored could see him." The translation "without seeing Him" carries the other side of the same idea — fearing a Lord you have never laid eyes on. Both meanings land in the same place: this is faith with no audience. Ibn Kathir cites here that the Prophet ﷺ mentioned **"a man who remembered Allah the Exalted while alone, and his eyes became tearful."** (The source quotes these words without naming a collection, so take them as the teaching of the Prophet ﷺ rather than as a citation you can trace to a named book.)

Everything in this description happens where nobody is watching: sins recalled in private, forgiveness sought in secret, fear of Allah when only He can see, tears in an empty room. The Qur'an's portrait of a person of Paradise is drawn almost entirely from his hidden life.

**"And brought a heart turned in repentance" (ayah 33).** The verb *jāʾa* ("came, brought") is striking: on that Day the heart is what you carry in your hands. Ibn Kathir says he will meet Allah on the Day of Resurrection with a heart turned to Him in repentance, **absolutely free of shirk**, and humbled to Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes Abu Bakr Warraq on the marks of the *munīb*: he always maintains respect for Allah, humbles himself before Him, and gives up his sensual and base desires.

## The invitation

**"Enter it in peace. This is the Day of eternal life!" (ayah 34).** *Bi-salām* — Ibn Kathir renders it "in peace and security" and opens it out: they will earn security from the torment of Allah, and — on Qatadah's explanation — **the angels of Allah will greet them with the *salām***. So the phrase is both a state and a sound: safety granted, and a welcome spoken at the gate.

*Yawm al-khulūd*, "the Day of eternal life," answers the quiet fear that shadows every joy — that it will end. Ibn Kathir spells out three layers: they will reside in Paradise forever and **never die**; they will **never be transferred out of it**; and they will **never even wish** to be transferred from it.

## "And with Us is more"

**"There they will have whatever they desire" (ayah 35).** Ibn Kathir: whatever delights they wish and desire, they will find brought before them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the emphasis on speed — brought forthwith, without any delay — and records, on the authority of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri in the *Musnad* of Ahmad, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "If anyone in Paradise wishes for children, the conception, delivery of the baby and its growth will all take place in a short span of time." Wishing and having collapse into one moment.

**Then the ayah goes past desire altogether: *wa ladaynā mazīd* — "and with Us is more."** Feel the echo. In ayah 30 the Fire asked, *hal min mazīd* — "are there any more?" — an appetite that could not be filled. Here the same word returns from Allah, but now as an offer rather than a demand: *ladaynā mazīd*, "and with Us there is even more." The hunger of Hell and the generosity of the Lord are set against each other in one word.

What is this "more"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that there are with Allah such desirable delights as **have not been conceived of by any man**, and which therefore no one could have wished or desired for — so they sit outside the "whatever they desire" of the first half of the ayah by definition. Ibn Kathir connects the phrase to Allah's words elsewhere, *"For those who have done good is the best and even more"* (10:26).

And the sources are explicit about what the greatest "more" is. Ibn Kathir notes that in the *Sahih*, Muslim recorded from Suhayb bin Sinan ar-Rumi that "more" refers to **looking at the Most Honorable Face of Allah**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from Anas and Jabir that "more" here refers to the greatest reward of enabling the people of Jannah to see Allah *bilā kayf* — "without 'how,' in an indescribable manner." We affirm the seeing as it was told to us and leave the "how" to Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, citing Qurtubi, that some reports narrate that the people of Paradise will see Allah on Friday.

So the passage that began with Paradise being brought near to those who had *taqwa* ends with something greater than Paradise: the sight of the One who made it.

## Who fills the Garden

Two hadith in Ibn Kathir's commentary here fill in the scale and the spirit of this promise.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Anas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that people will keep being thrown into Jahannam and it will keep saying, "Are there any more?" **until the Mighty Lord puts His Foot over it** — and then its corners will be collected together and it will say, "Enough, enough, by Your grace and compassion!" And **there will be sufficient empty space in Paradise until Allah creates another creation and makes them dwell in the empty parts of Paradise.** Muslim also collected this hadith. Hell must be pressed until it says "enough"; Paradise has room left over and Allah creates new beings to settle it. The two are not symmetrical, and the asymmetry is mercy. (Al-Bukhari records the same scene from Abu Hurayrah in shorter form: Jahannam will be asked, "Are you full?" and it will say, "Are there any more?" until the Lord, the Blessed and Most Honored, puts His Foot over it and it says, "Enough! Enough!")

Al-Bukhari also recorded from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that Paradise and the Fire quarreled. The Fire said, "I have been favored with the arrogant people and tyrants." Paradise said, "What is wrong with me that only the poor and humble people enter me?" Allah said to Paradise, **"You are My mercy, with which I grant mercy to those whom I will among My servants,"** and said to Hell, "You are My punishment which I inflict upon whom I wish from My servants, and I shall fill both of you" — and the hadith adds that Allah shall not be unjust to any one of His creatures.

That last clause matches what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws from ayah 29, just above our passage: "The Word is not changed with Me, and I am not a wrongdoer to My slaves" — Allah's decision is made and will certainly be implemented and never changed, and He will not punish anyone except on account of their sins after the proof has been established against them. That, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, is an absolutely fair and just decision. Paradise, by contrast, is called by Allah **"My mercy."** The four qualities in ayat 32–33 are the door His mercy chooses to come through.

## Living it

Read ayat 32 and 33 as a checklist of the private life, because that is what they are:

- **Return often, not once.** Ibn Masʿud, al-Shaʿbi and Mujahid describe a person who, alone and in secret, remembers what he did and asks Allah's forgiveness — and ʿUbaid ibn ʿUmair would have you close every sitting that way.
- **Keep guard.** As Ibn ʿAbbas has it: remember your sins so that you return and make amends, and guard the command of Allah — the covenant you made with Him — without breaking or betraying it.
- **Repent with intent.** Ibn Kathir's condition: sincere return, intending not to repeat the sin.
- **Build a life Allah alone can see.** Fear of Allah in secret, where only He can see; remembrance while alone; tears no one witnesses.
- **Bring a heart, not just a record.** Free of shirk, humbled, turned back to Him — and, as Abu Bakr Warraq said, having given up base desires.
- **A small, concrete start:** the four rakʿat of Ishraq early in the day, which the narration Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites from Qurtubi ties to both titles the ayah names.

And keep ayah 31 in view while you do it. Paradise is *ghayra baʿīd* — not far. Neither is the Day.

passages.title: Ruined generations and creation without fatigue
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Three ayat, one argument. Allah addresses the people who are denying the Prophet ﷺ and points them to history: nations far stronger than they were destroyed (ayah 36); that record is a reminder — but only for a certain kind of listener (ayah 37); and the One who did that is the One who created the heavens and the earth without any fatigue touching Him, which is why raising the dead is not beyond Him (ayah 38).

What holds the three together is a single movement from **the past**, to **the ear that hears it**, to **the power that guarantees the future**.

A note on where these ayat sit: Ibn Kathir places them under one heading that runs past our three ayat into ayat 39–40 — *"Warning the Disbelievers of the imminent Torment; commanding the Prophet ﷺ to pray and have Patience."* The second half of that heading belongs to the ayat after ours; what follows here covers only the warning. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān heads the same material simply *"Warning the Disbelievers of the imminent Torment."*

---

## Ayah 36 — stronger than you, and it did not save them

**"How many a generation We have destroyed before them, who were stronger in power than they."**

Ibn Kathir renders Allah's question as: "how many We have destroyed before these denying disbelievers?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the verse as **a rhetorical question posed to the unbelievers** — not a request for a figure, but a summons to look at a record.

Then note whom the Qur'an picks for the comparison. Not weaker peoples — **stronger** ones. Ibn Kathir explains *ashaddu minhum baṭshan* ("stronger in power than they") as: **they were more numerous, mightier than these, and they constructed on the earth and built on it more than these have.** Allah answers the deniers by pointing at civilisations that out-numbered them, out-muscled them and out-built them — and are gone.

### *Naqqabū* — they drilled their way through the land

The next phrase is one of the most vivid in the sūrah: **فَنَقَّبُوا فِي الْبِلَادِ** — *fa naqqabū fi'l-bilād*, "and they went about the land."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up. The verb *naqqabū* comes from *tanqīb*, which **literally means to make a hole, to perforate or pierce**. Idiomatically, Maʿārif says — citing al-Qāmūs — it connotes **to go away through distant land or country, to journey, to traverse**. So the picture is of people boring through the earth with their travelling: cutting routes, opening up country, leaving little unexplored.

The early authorities read that restlessness in two complementary ways:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās:** "They left the traces throughout the land." Their marks and works were scattered across the earth.
- **Qatādah:** "They travelled throughout the land seeking provisions through trade and business, **more than you have**." That last clause is the sting: the commercial reach of the deniers is modest next to nations already buried.

### *Maḥīṣ* — was there anywhere to run?

**هَلْ مِنْ مَحِيصٍ** — "Could they find any place of refuge?"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses *maḥīṣ* as **asylum, a place of refuge**, and draws the verse together: they were more numerous and mightier than you, and they travelled throughout the land for trade and business — **but they could not find shelter from their destined death. No land could give them shelter.**

Ibn Kathir presses the same point and then turns it on the listener. The meaning, he says, is: could they find a shelter from **Allah's decision and appointed destiny**? Did what they collected benefit them, or avert Allah's torment when it came to them on account of their denial of the Messengers? And then the application: **"Likewise, you will never be able to avert, avoid, or find refuge or shelter (from His torment)."**

There is a symmetry in the wording worth pausing on. The same verb that describes their mastery of the earth — they pierced through *the lands* — is immediately met by the question of whether any *land* would hide them. Movement, wealth and building can carry a people everywhere on the map, and, as Maʿārif puts it, still leave them with no shelter from what was decreed.

---

## Ayah 37 — who actually gets the lesson

**"Verily, therein is indeed a reminder for him who has a heart, or gives ear while he is heedful."**

Ibn Kathir's gloss on *dhikrā* is simply: **a reminder and a lesson.** Maʿārif heads its comment on this ayah *"Channels of Acquiring Knowledge"* — because the ayah names exactly **two doors** into that lesson.

### The first door: *liman kāna lahu qalb* — "for whoever has a heart"

Ibn Kathir explains "has a heart" as **"a sound understanding with which he comprehends"**, and reports from **Mujāhid** that it means **a good mind**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two readings from the scholars:

1. **Ibn ʿAbbās:** *qalb* here means *ʿaql*, **intellect** — because the centre of intellect is the heart.
2. **Some scholars of the Qur'an** say that "heart" here refers to **life**, because the axis of life is the heart.

Either way the conclusion Maʿārif draws is the same: **only the person who has life, or a sound understanding with which he comprehends, will be able to benefit from the advice and lesson of the Qur'an. The one devoid of intellect cannot benefit from it.**

### The second door: *alqā al-samʿ wa huwa shahīd* — "gives ear while present"

This is the more searching half of the ayah, and it is the one that concerns most of us most days.

Maʿārif explains the phrase *ilqāʾ al-samʿ* as **to listen to someone attentively**, and *shahīd* as **present**. Ibn Kathir describes such a person as one who **hears the speech, comprehends and understands it in his mind, and grasps its indications with his intellect.**

Then come two glosses that are almost uncomfortably precise:

- **Mujāhid** said that "gives ear" means **he does not talk to himself, but listens with an attentive heart.**
- **Ad-Daḥḥāk** commented: "The Arabs would say that someone has given ear when he hears with his ears, **while his heart is present and not absent**." Ibn Kathir notes that **ath-Thawrī and several others** said similarly.

Mujāhid's phrase — *he does not talk to himself* — is the condition in five words. What it rules out is not deafness but the inner monologue running underneath the recitation: composing the reply, rehearsing the objection, drifting elsewhere. The ears receive; the heart, in Ad-Daḥḥāk's terms, is absent.

### Two kinds of people who benefit

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the ayah's conclusion plainly. **Two types of people benefit:**

1. **The one who has the mind and the intellect**, who understands it in his mind and accepts it.
2. **The one who gives his ears and listens** to the Divine verses **with an attentive heart, while his heart is present and not absent.**

Maʿārif then cites **Mazharī's** interpretation: the first type are called *kāmilīn* — the thoroughly proficient members of the Islamic community. The second type are their followers and sincere seekers of Reality, who are under the direction of a spiritual guide and who, **on account of their sincerity and purity of heart**, accept the teachings of the religion.

That is a generous reading, and worth holding onto. Not everyone will be among the *kāmilīn*. But the door of sincere, attentive listening stands open beside it — and the ayah puts the two side by side, joined by "or," as two routes to the same reminder.

---

## Ayah 38 — six days, and nothing of fatigue

**"And indeed We created the heavens and the earth and all that is between them in six Days, and nothing of fatigue touched Us."**

Why does this sentence appear right here, after a warning about destroyed nations? Ibn Kathir answers directly: it **is emphasis on the Resurrection, because He Who is able to create the heavens and earth without fatigue is surely able to resurrect the dead.**

This argument from the greater to the lesser is one Ibn Kathir illustrates by gathering three parallel ayat:

- **"Do they not see that Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth, and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes, He surely is Able to do all things."** (46:33)
- **"The creation of the heavens and the earth is indeed greater than the creation of mankind."** (40:57)
- **"Are you more difficult to create, or is the heaven that He constructed?"** (79:27)

A person who accepts that the skies were raised is being asked a simple question: on what grounds is the raising of one human being the harder job?

### "Nothing of fatigue touched Us"

The Arabic is **وَمَا مَسَّنَا مِن لُّغُوبٍ** — *wa mā massanā min lughūb*. Ibn Kathir's comment is short and total: it indicates that **no sleep, exhaustion or weariness affects Him.**

Notice the shape of the wording: not merely "We were not tired," but *nothing of fatigue **touched** Us* — the very brush of tiredness is denied. Among creatures, building costs something and the greater the project the greater the exhaustion. What this ayah denies of Allah, on Ibn Kathir's reading, is exactly that: sleep, exhaustion, weariness. He is above every one of them.

### Why the denial was needed

Ibn Kathir records from **Qatādah** that this closing phrase came down as a rebuttal. Qatādah said that **the Jews said Allah created the heavens and earth in six days and then rested on the seventh day, the Sabbath — which is why they call it a holiday — and that Allah then sent down a denial of their statement and false opinion.**

So the ayah does two jobs at once. It corrects a claim about Allah — that creating cost Him something He had to recover from — and, in correcting it, it removes the excuse of the one who doubts the Resurrection. If creation did not tire Him, there is no reason to imagine the second creation will be beyond Him.

---

## Living it

**Read the ruins.** Ayah 36 is not ancient history for its own sake. Ibn Kathir turns it directly on the reader: what they collected did not benefit them or avert Allah's torment when it came — and *likewise* you will never be able to avert, avoid, or find refuge from His torment. They were more numerous, mightier, greater builders, further travelled. None of it was shelter.

**Audit how you listen.** Ayah 37 makes attention a condition of benefit. Before the Qur'an is recited, before the reminder — Mujāhid's test is the one to apply: *am I still talking to myself?* Ad-Daḥḥāk's phrase is the target: **hearing with the ears, while the heart is present and not absent.**

**Let ayah 38 settle your doubt about the Hour.** The One who created the heavens and the earth without fatigue touching Him is, as Ibn Kathir says, surely able to resurrect the dead — and no sleep, exhaustion or weariness affects Him.

passages.title: Patience, praise, and the Day of Emergence
passages.tafsir:
These seven ayat close Sūrah Qāf. They take a Prophet ﷺ who is being contradicted and mocked, and hand him two things: a discipline to hold onto now — patience and prayer — and a scene to keep before his eyes: the moment the earth splits and everyone who ever lived is summoned out of it. What binds the passage together is that pairing — **what you do in the meantime (39–40), and what is coming (41–44)** — closed in ayah 45 by a word of comfort about what is, and is not, his responsibility.

The passage grows straight out of ayah 38, just before it: Allah created the heavens and the earth and everything between them in six days, "and nothing of fatigue touched Us." Ibn Kathir explains that this is stated as an emphasis on the Resurrection — the One able to create the heavens and the earth without fatigue is surely able to resurrect the dead. He records from Qatadah that the words also came down in denial of the claim that Allah created the heavens and earth in six days and then rested on the seventh; "and nothing of fatigue touched Us" indicates that no sleep, exhaustion or weariness affects Him. Hold that in mind, because everything that follows rests on it.

## "So be patient with what they say" (39)

Ibn Kathir says this is spoken in reference to those who deny the Prophet ﷺ: he is ordered to be patient with them and to turn away from them in a good way. Notice how specific the trial is. It is not persecution by the sword that is named here but *what they say* — the sneering, the accusations, the wearing-down of words. That is the pressure this passage is built to answer.

And notice the medicine prescribed. Not argument, not retaliation — **worship**. The very next word is *wa sabbiḥ*.

## What "tasbīḥ" actually means (39)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up. The command *sabbiḥ* comes from the verbal noun *tasbīḥ*, which originally means **to declare or proclaim the purity of Allah** — to hold Him far above every defect and every lie told about Him. And, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, this comprehends both the verbal declaration or proclamation *and* the worship, such as prayer.

That double range is why the commentators read the two time-markers in ayah 39 the way they do. Because tasbīḥ takes in prayer, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some scholars say tasbīḥ before sunrise refers to the morning prayer and tasbīḥ before sunset to ʿAṣr, the late afternoon prayer. Its own rendering of the ayah keeps both halves of the command visible: "and proclaim His purity along with your Lord's praise before sunrise and before sunset."

Ibn Kathir places this in its historical moment. Before the Isrāʼ — the Night Journey — there were **two ordained prayers**: one before the rising of the sun at dawn, and one before sunset in the evening. Standing at night in prayer (*qiyām al-layl*) was for a time a command for the Prophet ﷺ and his followers, and was later abrogated for the Ummah. Then, during the Isrāʼ, Allah abrogated all of the previous orders for prayer by ordaining the five daily prayers — which still include Fajr before sunrise and ʿAṣr in the late afternoon. So this ayah is a window into the Muslim day before the five prayers were given: two appointments, one at each end of the light.

## The full moon and the two prayers (39)

Ibn Kathir reports that Imam Ahmad recorded from Jarīr ibn ʿAbdullāh: "When we were sitting with the Prophet ﷺ, he looked at the full moon and said, 'Certainly you will be brought before your Lord and will see Him as you see this moon, and you will have no trouble in seeing Him. So, if you can avoid missing the prayer before the sunrise and the prayer before sunset, you must do so.'" He then recited this very ayah — *and glorify the praises of your Lord, before the rising of the sun and before its setting*. Ibn Kathir notes that the Two Ṣaḥīḥs and the rest of the Group collected this hadith through the chain of Ismāʿīl; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites it from Bukhārī and Muslim, in a wording that names the two prayers explicitly as ʿAṣr and Fajr.

Two things are worth pausing over. First, what the Prophet ﷺ told them they were heading towards: they will be brought before their Lord and will see Him, with no trouble in seeing Him.

Second, the pairing itself. He looked at the moon, spoke of that meeting, and in the same breath told them to guard the two prayers that bracket the daylight — and Jarīr's report closes with the Prophet ﷺ reciting this ayah over that instruction.

## Wider tasbīḥ: morning and evening (39)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that although according to the majority of commentators *tasbīḥ* in the verse refers to ṣalāh, the general words of tasbīḥ also include all those invocations whose recitation authentic ahadith encourage at the time of morning and evening. It cites two reports from Abū Hurayrah recorded by Bukhārī and Muslim: that whoever recites *Subḥān Allāh* a hundred times morning and evening — no one will bring, on the Day of Judgment, a virtuous act better than it, except those who recite the same or more; and that whoever recites *Subḥān Allāhi wa bi-ḥamdih* a hundred times in a day will have his sins forgiven, even though they may be more than the waves of the sea.

Notice how closely the wording of that second remembrance sits beside the wording of the ayah itself.

## Night, and the ends of the prostrations (40)

Ayah 40 extends the same discipline into the dark, and into the moments just after worship.

**"And glorify Him during part of the night"** — Ibn Kathir says this means *pray to Him*, and connects it to Allah's word, *And in some parts of the night offer the Ṣalāh with it, as an additional prayer for you. It may be that your Lord will raise you to Maqām Maḥmūd* (17:79) — the Praiseworthy Station. The night, which for the exhausted is only rest, becomes for him a place of ascent.

**"and after the prostrations"** (*wa adbār as-sujūd*) — here the commentators record two readings, and both are held by weighty authorities:

1. **The remembrances said after the prayers.** Ibn Abī Najīḥ reported from Mujāhid that Ibn ʿAbbās said *adbār as-sujūd* refers to tasbīḥ — glorifying Allah's praises — after the prayers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives Mujāhid's reading in the same direction: *sujūd* here refers to the five obligatory prayers, and "the ends of the prostrations" refers to all those tasbīḥāt which authentic ahadith encourage us to recite after every prayer.
2. **The two rakʿahs after Maghrib.** Ibn Kathir reports this from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, his son al-Ḥasan, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayrah and Abū Umāmah, may Allah be pleased with them — and it is also the saying of Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ash-Shaʿbī, an-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Qatādah and others. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likewise notes the phrase could refer to the supererogatory prayers performed after the obligatory ones, as authentic Traditions testify.

Ibn Kathir sets both readings down without discarding either, and by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account authentic ahadith encourage both practices. There is no need to force a choice.

### The hadith of the poor migrants

For the first reading, Ibn Kathir cites a hadith collected in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs. Abū Hurayrah said: some poor migrants came and said, "O Allah's Messenger! The wealthy people will get higher grades and will have permanent enjoyment." He ﷺ asked, "Why is that?" They said, "They pray as we do, fast as we do, yet they give charity, but we cannot. They free slaves, but we cannot." He ﷺ said: "Shall I tell you about something that, if you did it, you would catch up with those who have surpassed you, and nobody would be better than you except those who would do the same? Say *Subḥān Allāh*, *Alḥamdulillāh* and *Allāhu Akbar*, thirty-three times each after every prayer." Later they came back and said their wealthy brethren had heard of what they did and were doing the same. He ﷺ said: "This is a favour and grace of Allah, and He grants it to whom He wills."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same practice from Abū Hurayrah in Bukhārī and Muslim with the completing formula: after every obligatory prayer, thirty-three *Subḥān Allāh*, thirty-three *Alḥamdulillāh*, thirty-three *Allāhu Akbar*, and once *lā ilāha illallāhu waḥdahu lā sharīka lah, lahul-mulku wa lahul-ḥamdu wa huwa ʿalā kulli shayʼin qadīr* — and all his sins will be forgiven, even though they may be equal to the waves of the sea.

Read that beside the passage's opening. A man with nothing to give but his tongue is not left behind.

## "And listen!" — the Day arrives (41–42)

At ayah 41 the tone changes completely. Ibn Kathir renders *wastamiʿ* as *And listen*, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ — listen for the Day when the caller calls to the gathering for the Day of Judgement.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, from Ibn ʿAsākir on the authority of Zaid ibn Jābir Shāfiʿī, that this "caller" is the angel Isrāfīl, who will stand on the Dome of the Rock (aṣ-Ṣakhrah) and address all the dead people of the entire world: "O you rotten bones! O you decomposed skins! O you scattered hair! Listen, Allah commands you to reassemble to render account of your actions." The scene depicts what follows the second blowing of the Trumpet.

And **"from a near place"**? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the angel's voice will reach everybody who rises from death anywhere on the surface of the earth, and each will feel as though the angel had called him from a nearby place. ʿIkrimah said the voice will be heard as if someone were speaking to us in our ears. Other scholars (cited via Qurṭubī) took "a near place" to mean the Dome of the Rock itself, because it is the centre of the earth, equidistant from all sides of the globe. Either way the point lands: **no one is at the back of that crowd.** The summons is not general and distant; it is at your ear.

Ayah 42 names the sound: *aṣ-Ṣayḥah bil-ḥaqq*, the Blast, in truth. Ibn Kathir says this refers to the blowing in the Trumpet, which will bring forth the truth that most of them discounted and denied. *Bil-ḥaqq* is a quiet verdict on the whole argument of the surah: the thing they discounted turns out to be the thing that is real. And so it is *yawm al-khurūj* — the Day of Coming Out, from the graves.

## How the dead are raised (43–44)

Ayah 43 is the axis: *It is certainly We Who give life and cause death, and to Us is the final return.* Ibn Kathir comments that Allah is He Who starts creation and then brings it back to life, and the latter is easier for Him; to Him is the final return of all creations, and at that time He will recompense each according to his or her deeds — good for good and evil for evil.

Then ayah 44 — the earth splitting, the dead hurrying out. Ibn Kathir describes the sequence: Allah will send down rain from the sky, and from that rain the bodies will grow while they are in their graves, just as the seed grows in soil in the aftermath of rain. When the bodies grow to their full strength, Allah will command the angel Isrāfīl and he will blow in the Trumpet a second time. The souls, enclosed in a hole in the Trumpet, will depart from it and fly between the heavens and the earth, and Allah will declare: "By My grace and power, each soul shall return to the body that it used to inhabit." Every soul will return to its body — entering it, Ibn Kathir says, just as poison enters the body — then the earth will be uncovered from above them, and they will all stand and head towards the Reckoning place, hastening to obey the command of Allah.

He sets other ayat alongside it: *Hastening towards the caller. The disbelievers will say: "This is a hard Day"* (54:8), and *On the Day when He will call you, and you will answer with words of His praise and obedience, and you will think that you have stayed but a little while* (17:52) — a whole lifetime shrinking, in hindsight, to a moment.

In the Ṣaḥīḥ, it is recorded that Anas said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"The earth will open up first around me."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that this hurrying will be towards Syria, where the Dome of the Rock is situated and where Isrāfīl will stand and call the people on the Day of Judgment. It cites Jāmiʿ Tirmidhī, on the authority of Muʿāwiyah ibn Ḥayadah, that the Prophet ﷺ pointed towards Syria and said: "From here towards that you will be raised, some riding, and others on foot, and yet others will be dragged on the faces on the Day of Judgment."

The ayah then closes with the line the whole passage has been building to: *That is an easy gathering for Us.* Ibn Kathir: bringing them back to life is easy for Us and effortless — as Allah says, *And Our commandment is but one, as the twinkling of an eye* (54:50), and *The creation of you all and the resurrection of you all are only as of a single person* (31:28). All of humanity, first to last, costs Him no more than one soul.

## The last word: comfort, and the limits of the messenger (45)

*We know best what they say.* Ibn Kathir explains: Our knowledge is all-encompassing of the denial that the idolaters are confronting you with — **so do not be concerned.** Nothing said against him goes unheard or unrecorded. He is not required to carry it; it is already carried. Compare Allah's words, *Indeed, We know that your breast is straitened at what they say. So glorify the praises of your Lord and be of those who prostrate themselves. And worship your Lord until there comes unto you the certainty* (15:97–99) — the identical prescription: hurtful words met with prostration.

*And you are not there to compel them* — *wa mā anta ʿalayhim bi-jabbār*. Ibn Kathir: it is not you who forces them to accept the guidance; this is not a part of your mission. He gathers the parallels: *Your duty is only to convey the Message, and on Us is the reckoning* (13:40); *So remind them — you are only one who reminds. You are not a dictator over them* (88:21–22); *Not upon you is their guidance, but Allah guides whom He wills* (2:272); *Verily, you guide not whom you like, but Allah guides whom He wills* (28:56).

*But remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning.* Ibn Kathir: convey the Message of your Lord, for only those who fear Allah and dread His torment, and hope in His promise, will remember and heed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the balance explicit — the message of the Qur'an is to be conveyed to the entire mankind, to all and sundry; but only those who fear Allah and dread His torment will remember and heed. Universal delivery, selective response. That distinction spares the caller both arrogance and despair.

## Living it

- **Answer insult with tasbīḥ, not argument.** When you are spoken about unjustly, the ayah does not tell you to compose a reply; it tells you to proclaim your Lord's purity along with His praise.
- **Guard Fajr and ʿAṣr** — the two prayers this ayah was recited over, and the two the Prophet ﷺ named as he spoke of being brought before your Lord.
- **Keep the after-prayer remembrance.** Thirty-three, thirty-three, thirty-three — the practice that let the poor migrants catch up with those who had surpassed them.
- **Let ayah 41 stay near.** The call comes "from a near place" — as if spoken into your ear, and directed at you personally.
- **Do not try to compel anyone.** Deliver, be sincere, and leave guidance to the One who owns it.

Qatadah, both commentaries tell us, used to make this very ayah into a supplication: *"O Allah! Make us among those who fear Your threat and hope for Your promise, O Barr, O Raḥīm."* Ibn Kathir's text explains those two names as he gives them — *Barr* (Subtle, Kind, Courteous, and Generous) and *Raḥīm* (the Most Merciful); Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the first as "O the One who fulfills His promise." That is the fitting way to end the surah — asking to be counted among the people its last ayah describes.
